newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss franc gains seen modest despite EMU concerns.
newsitem.headline: Swiss franc gains seen modest despite EMU concerns.

text.p: The Swiss franc's ability to profit from negative developments tied to European economic and monetary union (EMU) appears to have diminished in recent months, currency analysts say.
Amid recent speculation the single currency plan may be postponed, the Swiss franc has lately gained somewhat versus the mark, but the gains appear limited.
Union Bank of Switzerland economist Markus Allenspach said based on an interest rate model the Swiss franc recently had enjoyed no safe-haven bonus at all.
But Swiss investors would likely repatriate money if a new crisis of confidence in the single currency project emerges.
"If Switzerland decides to repatriate, it has quite an impact," Allenspach said, adding Switzerland at the end of 1995 had net foreign assets of about 350 billion Swiss francs.
UBS forecasts the Swiss franc to be lower in the next six months versus the dollar and mark but over 12 months it expects the franc to be back up again at roughly current levels.
"In the spring of 1998 we will have the European Union summit, and there will be a lot of uncertainty ahead of such an event. This is going to boost the Swiss franc," he said.
UBS also expects the Swiss economy to improve in 12 months.

The franc is seen unattractive due to Swiss interest rates, the lowest in Europe, and Switzerland's frail economy. Analysts believe the Swiss National Bank (SNB) would be quick to lower interest rates if there is significant franc appreciation.

Meanwhile, Swiss investors have been tempted by higher yields abroad, as the memory of sharp franc gains fade. When nervousness about EMU sent tremors through markets in 1995, some economists forecast then the Swiss franc, which dipped to 1.10 to the dollar, was on its way to dollar parity.
But the franc failed to hit dollar parity and the dollar has since recovered to between 1.40 to 1.50 Swiss francs.

On a long-term basis the Swiss franc has also dropped against the mark to current levels around 86 centimes. That compared with a level of just above 80.00 Swiss centimes in late 1995. In the past days, the franc has gained again versus the mark, which had traded as high as 87.77 February 20.
"I think the Swiss franc is benefiting from the perception that EMU might be in trouble," said Adam Beaudin, currency analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston.
"When EMU is under pressure the SFR does benefit from safe haven status. If Europe fails to unite, Switzerland suddenly looks like a relative island of stability," Beaudin said.
"If we go through with EMU, in the later stages of that, Switzerland looks isolated," he added.
Latest EMU tremors included comments by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel that entrance criteria played a bigger role than a timetable for EMU.

Waigel on Monday reiterated Germany's 1997 budget deficit should be 2.9 percent of gross domestic product, just below the 3.0 percent ceiling countries must respect to qualify for EMU in 1999. Bundsbank board member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said he doubted this and said EMU may this have to be postponed.

"I think you have to allow for more room on the downside" in terms of mark/Swiss, Beaudin said. He said a level of 84.00 to 85.00 centimes may be possible but said in relative terms the declines were not likely to be as great as two years ago.

Credit Suisse economist Stefan Buchli said there could be some scope for Swiss franc gains versus the mark, the EMU lynchpin, over a 12-month period, but the mark may not fall as much as it did against the Swiss franc over the past year if serious problems arise on the road to the joint currency.

"We forecast mark/Swiss at 86.00 in 12 months. We could see it potentially going as low as 84.00 on EMU tension. But we doubt it will go as low as last year," said Buchli. -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
